chapters.title: 1 Background
chapters.summary:
David Ogilvy's entry into the world of advertising was a circuitous journey through a series of disparate and formative experiences, each of which he would later draw upon as essential ingredients in his unique and powerful philosophy. Born in London in 1911 and educated at the prestigious Fettes College and later at Oxford, he was famously expelled, an event he recounts not with bitterness but with a sense of liberated opportunity. His subsequent years were a deliberate immersion in the practical world: he trained as a chef at the Hôtel Majestic in Paris, learning the disciplines of precision, timing, and presentation that would later define his approach to advertising campaigns.

He then embarked on a three-year stint as a door-to-door salesman for AGA cooking stoves in Scotland. This experience was transformative; he not only mastered the art of persuasion through direct conversation but also produced the celebrated AGA sales manual, a document of such clear, logical, and persuasive instruction that it became legendary in sales circles and demonstrated his innate talent for breaking down complex propositions into simple, actionable steps.

His time at the Gallup organization in America was perhaps the most intellectually pivotal period of his pre-advertising life. Hired by Dr. George Gallup, he spent years conducting audience research and polling, immersing himself in the nascent science of understanding consumer motivation through data. This empirical foundation—placing the consumer's reality above the advertiser's assumptions—would become the bedrock of his entire career. During World War II, he served in British Intelligence in Washington, an experience that honed his skills in psychology, persuasion, and strategic communication.

After the war, he briefly considered a life of farming in Pennsylvania Amish country before the pull of commerce and communication proved irresistible. In 1948, he co-founded the agency Hewitt, Ogilvy, Benson & Mather in New York. The launch was audacious: they started with no clients and a team largely borrowed from London's S.H. Benson agency. His early breakthroughs, however, were stunning in their originality and effectiveness. The Schweppes campaign featuring Commander Whitehead's distinctive beard, the unforgettable Rolls-Royce headline "at 60 miles an hour the loudest noise comes from the electric clock," and the repositioning of Dove soap as a non-drying product for dry skin all demonstrated his unique blend of deep research, compelling storytelling, and strategic positioning. He built his agency not on flamboyant pitches and ego-driven creativity, but on the disciplined, research-driven approach he had honed at Gallup, proving that a profound respect for the consumer's intelligence could produce advertising that was both more commercially effective and more enduring than work based on mere artistic impulse.
chapters.takeaway: Diverse experience—selling, research, writing—compounds into an edge; ground creativity in facts about customers.
takeaways: Diverse experience—selling, research, writing—compounds into an edge; ground creativity in facts about customers.
A foundation in research and data provides a decisive competitive advantage over intuition and guesswork.
Practical, hands-on sales experience teaches the fundamentals of persuasion that no theoretical training can replace.

chapters.title: 2 How to Manage an Advertising Agency
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy's management philosophy is rooted in a simple, powerful, and often ignored premise: the quality of an agency is determined exclusively by the quality of its people. He famously declared, "If you always hire people who are smaller than you, we shall become a company of dwarfs. If you always hire people who are bigger than you, we shall become a company of giants." This principle of hiring superior talent is the non-negotiable cornerstone. He believed managers must have the courage to delegate authority boldly, empowering subordinates to make significant decisions and take real ownership of their work. Micromanagement, in his view, is the enemy of both efficiency and creativity, as it stifles initiative and signals a lack of trust.

He outlines a series of practical disciplines for running an efficient and effective agency: conduct productive meetings that start and end on time with clear agendas, communicate through clear and concise memoranda that get to the point, and make decisions promptly to avoid the paralysis of over-analysis. He stressed the non-negotiable standard of quality, arguing that tolerating second-rate work demoralizes the first-rate people you've worked so hard to attract. Recognition and feedback must be handled with care and wisdom—praise should be given publicly to boost morale and reinforce desired behaviors, while criticism should be delivered privately to preserve dignity and encourage learning.

Ogilvy was deeply suspicious of office politics and empire-building, which he saw as corrosive distractions. He favored flat organizational structures where the hierarchy served the work, not the other way around. The best work, he believed, should always triumph over internal politics and personal agendas. His ideal manager was a craftsman, an "ad man who still writes ads," staying intimately close to the product and the creative output, rather than an administrator detached in an ivory tower. This hands-on approach ensured that standards remained high, the agency's core mission—creating great advertising—was never lost in bureaucratic complexity, and that the creative product remained the ultimate source of pride and profit.
chapters.takeaway: Hire people better than yourself, delegate boldly, and enforce high standards without crushing morale.
takeaways: Hire people better than yourself, delegate boldly, and enforce high standards without crushing morale.
Tolerating mediocre work drives away your best employees and creates a culture of settling.
Effective leaders are hands-on practitioners who stay connected to the core craft of the agency.

chapters.title: 3 How to Get Clients
chapters.summary:
Winning clients when you have none is the ultimate test of an agency's credibility, resourcefulness, and skill. Ogilvy's strategy was multifaceted, combining long-term reputation building with meticulous, almost forensic, pitch preparation. He understood that new business could be attracted by demonstrating expertise and thought leadership long before a direct approach was made. His agency's famous "house ads" and his own prolific output of published speeches and books served as a powerful form of intellectual bait, showcasing his thinking and attracting like-minded potential clients who resonated with his principles.

When pursuing a specific account, he advocated for exhaustive, deep-dive research into the prospect's business, their market position, their competitors, and their internal challenges. The goal was to enter the pitch room knowing more about their problems than the incumbent agency did. Pitches needed to be utterly specific and tailored, presenting concrete ideas developed for the client's unique situation rather than generic portfolio pieces or recycled ideas from other accounts. This specificity and preparation demonstrated genuine competence, serious intent, and a respect for the client's particular business. He also valued honesty and candor above all else; openly admitting an agency's weaknesses or past mistakes could disarm skepticism and build trust far more effectively than an improbable facade of perfection.

He acknowledged the significant role of luck—good timing, warm referrals from satisfied clients, and the momentum generated by early campaign successes like Schweppes all created a virtuous cycle. However, he counseled against desperate or undiscriminating tactics. Not every client is desirable; some accounts are more trouble, more demanding, or less profitable than they are worth. Similarly, an agency should never pitch for business it cannot serve with genuine excellence, as overextension leads to poor work and damaged reputations. Ultimately, the most powerful and convincing pitch is the work itself. Presenting advertising of such quality, insight, and originality that it proves your competence beyond any argument is the surest and most enduring way to win a client's trust, respect, and business.
chapters.takeaway: Win clients by demonstrating deep knowledge of their business and presenting brilliant work in the pitch itself.
takeaways: Win clients by demonstrating deep knowledge of their business and presenting brilliant work in the pitch itself.
Published thought leadership and a consistent public voice attract potential clients organically.
Candor and honesty in the pitching process build more authentic trust than exaggerated claims of perfection.

chapters.title: 4 How to Keep Clients
chapters.summary:
While winning new clients is a celebrated and glamorous skill, Ogilvy argues that keeping them is an even greater, more nuanced, and more important art. It relies less on sporadic bursts of creative brilliance and more on the consistent, daily management of the relationship. He kept major clients like Shell and American Express for decades by making them feel secure, informed, and valued. This security was built on three pillars: absolute transparency, constant and open communication, and a relentless focus on measurable business results.

He advised agency leaders to deliver bad news to clients themselves, directly, immediately, and without flinching, rather than letting them hear it from a third party or discover it through poor performance metrics. No surprises. Constant, proactive communication was essential—keeping the top client leader informed directly, socializing with their senior team to build personal rapport and trust, and taking the time to understand the internal politics and personal ambitions of their organization so the agency could navigate them effectively. Successes should be measured not in creative awards but in concrete sales lifts and market share gains, and credit for those successes should be generously shared with the client, making them the hero of the story.

Ogilvy was clear-eyed and unequivocal about the limits of this accommodationist approach. When a client demanded work that violated the agency's professional standards, ethical principles, or long-term strategic advice, the agency must be prepared to resign the account rather than compromise its integrity. He cited personal examples of having done so, even with large accounts. The overarching principle is one of stewardship and fiduciary duty: an agency must treat the client's money as if it were its own, investing it wisely and frugally. This mindset of fiscal responsibility and shared fate is what ultimately forges the deepest trust and transforms a vendor-client relationship into a true, enduring, and mutually profitable partnership.
chapters.takeaway: Keep clients through candor, constant communication, measurable results, and treating their money like your own.
takeaways: Keep clients through candor, constant communication, measurable results, and treating their money like your own.
Proactively delivering bad news prevents larger crises and demonstrates true partnership.
Willingness to resign over principle ultimately strengthens professional respect and long-term trust.

chapters.title: 5 How to Be a Good Client
chapters.summary:
Inverting the perspective, Ogilvy offers essential and often neglected guidance for advertisers on how to extract maximum value from their agency partners. The foundation is selecting the right agency through a rigorous, objective, and disciplined evaluation process, and then backing that decision with unwavering commitment and loyalty. He points to exemplary clients like Unilever and General Foods, whose structured processes, clear expectations, and long-term perspective consistently elicited outstanding and effective work from their agencies.

A good client's primary responsibility is to provide a thorough, complete, and honest brief. This includes not just the immediate assignment, but the full picture: market facts, strategic objectives, long-term brand ambitions, competitive pressures, and any internal constraints. Once this brief is delivered, the client must then exhibit the discipline to resist the temptation to micromanage the creative execution. Constant meddling, second-guessing, and personal taste overriding strategy leads inevitably to safe, soulless, and ineffective work. Instead, clients should demand research-based justifications for creative recommendations, ensuring decisions are grounded in evidence and consumer insight rather than the shifting preferences of internal committees.

He delivers a sharp and lasting critique of committee-based approval processes, which he believes sand off all distinction, edge, and originality, producing advertising that is a "camel—a horse designed by a committee." Good clients avoid this by designating clear, empowered decision-makers. They also demonstrate loyalty, resisting the impulse to change agencies impulsively over a single campaign's performance or to squeeze agency fees so aggressively that the agency can no longer afford to invest the time, talent, and research required to produce great work. Paying agencies fairly and promptly, sharing long-term business plans openly, and rewarding risk-taking are all hallmarks of a client who fosters a partnership capable of producing genuinely great, effective, and enduring advertising.
chapters.takeaway: Brief thoroughly, decide decisively, pay fairly, and resist committees that turn bold ideas into camels.
takeaways: Brief thoroughly, decide decisively, pay fairly, and resist committees that turn bold ideas into camels.
Providing a complete brief and then granting creative freedom is the foundation of a productive partnership.
Committee-based approvals dilute creative ideas and produce ineffective, bland, and forgettable advertising.

chapters.title: 6 How to Build Great Campaigns
chapters.summary:
At the heart of Ogilvy's entire philosophy lies the concept of the "big idea" and the strategic discipline of positioning. He asserts with conviction, "Unless your campaign contains a big idea, it will pass like a ship in the night." A big idea is a clear, compelling, and differentiated positioning of the product in the consumer's mind—a promise that is both meaningful and singular. Examples like Dove's "for dry skin" and Volkswagen's "Think Small" are masterclasses in this powerful clarity. He insists on the courage to commit to one such positioning and to stay with it for decades, allowing the compounding power of repetition to build formidable and unshakable brand equity, as seen with Marlboro Country and Schweppes' Commander Whitehead.

He lays out concrete, non-negotiable rules for building such powerful campaigns. Start by clearly defining the consumer's specific problem and then present the product as the unique and effective solution. Use news and information, because consumers are fundamentally hungry for facts that help them make decisions, not empty slogans. The headline must deliver the whole selling message, as it is read by five times as many people as the body copy. Every advertisement must pass a personal test: it must be something you would be proud to show your own family, ensuring a baseline of quality, honesty, and respect for the viewer.

He champions research-tested claims over empty superlatives, arguing that specific, verifiable facts are infinitely more persuasive than vague boasts. The long-term view is essential and non-negotiable; twenty years of consistent, image-building repetition is vastly more effective and more economical than chasing fleeting creative trends or producing flashy, disconnected one-offs. Campaigns succeed not through novelty in each individual execution, but through the relentless, disciplined reinforcement of a single, powerful, and differentiated idea until it becomes indelibly etched in the public consciousness as the very definition of the product.
chapters.takeaway: Find one big positioning idea, commit to it for decades, and let repetition compound your brand.
takeaways: Find one big positioning idea, commit to it for decades, and let repetition compound your brand.
A big idea must clearly position the product and solve a specific, meaningful consumer problem.
Long-term consistency in messaging builds far stronger brand equity than frequent, flashy changes.

chapters.title: 7 How to Write Potent Copy
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy approached copywriting not as a mystical or innate art but as a rigorous, disciplined, and fundamentally learnable craft governed by clear principles and hard evidence. He placed paramount importance on the headline, declaring it does "the heavy lifting" in any advertisement. A headline must promise a clear benefit to the reader, include the brand name for immediate identification, and be relentlessly and systematically tested. He noted with characteristic directness that five times as many people read headlines as read body copy, making it the single most important element of an advertisement and the key to unlocking the rest of the message.

His stylistic commandments are legendary for their clarity and directness: write the way you naturally talk, using short words and short sentences to maximize comprehension and impact. Avoid industry jargon, hyperbole, and vague, empty superlatives like "great," "amazing," or "innovative." Instead, anchor your copy firmly in concrete, specific, and verifiable facts. His famous Rolls-Royce headline is the ultimate example: a single, specific, verifiable fact that sells more effectively than any flowery adjective ever could. He advocates using testimonials from real, identifiable users, citing specific numbers whenever possible to add credibility, and telling a story that engages the reader's imagination and emotions.

Editing is where good copy becomes great and potent. Ogilvy was a ferocious and obsessive rewriter; he famously produced 19 different headlines for the Rolls-Royce ad before settling on the winner. He advised cutting ruthlessly and mercilessly until every single word pulls its weight and contributes to the message. Avoid using more than a few typefaces to maintain visual clarity, and keep paragraphs short for ease of reading. Always end your copy on your strongest and most compelling point, leaving the reader with a powerful final impression. Underpinning all of this is a foundation of research: "Advertising people who ignore research are as dangerous as generals who ignore decodes of enemy signals." The copywriter's job is to translate research insights into persuasive, specific, and engaging language that connects with the reader's reality.
chapters.takeaway: Write fact-rich, conversational copy with benefit-driven headlines, and edit relentlessly until it sings.
takeaways: Write fact-rich, conversational copy with benefit-driven headlines, and edit relentlessly until it sings.
Headlines are the most critical element and should promise a clear benefit and include the brand name.
Specific facts and concrete details are far more persuasive than vague, superlative-filled language.

chapters.title: 8 How to Illustrate Advertisements and Posters
chapters.summary:
For Ogilvy, illustration was never mere decoration or an afterthought; it was a vital and integral component of the persuasive argument itself. The primary job of a picture is to attract the target reader's attention and to communicate the core selling message instantly, clearly, and powerfully, often before a single word is read. He advocated strongly and consistently for photography over illustration, believing that photographs could create "story appeal"—a sense of narrative, context, and humanity that draws the viewer in and makes the product feel real and desirable. His masterstroke was the Hathaway shirt campaign featuring a distinguished older gentleman in an eye-patch. The image was simultaneously intriguing, elegant, and unexpected, making a commodity product like a white shirt iconic by imbuing it with a sense of character and backstory.

Illustrations and photographs must have a direct, logical, and obvious relationship to the headline's promise. A clever but irrelevant image wastes the reader's attention and creates confusion. Show the product in use whenever possible, allowing the reader to visualize themselves owning and using it. Demonstrations, especially compelling before-and-after sequences, remain among the most powerful and credible persuasive tools available. For posters, where the viewer has only seconds to absorb the message, the rule is absolute simplicity: one single idea, readable at speed from a passing car, and memorable at a brief glance. His Schweppes posters, featuring the distinctive bottle and Commander Whitehead, are textbook examples of this powerful simplicity.

He provided practical technical guidance that remains sound: place a caption directly under photographs, as it is read far more frequently than body copy. Maintain consistent art direction across an entire campaign so that individual ads are immediately recognizable as part of a cohesive series, building familiarity and brand recall over time. Avoid clutter at all costs, as every extraneous element dilutes the message. Always test different visuals against each other where feasible to determine which is most effective. Ultimately, the picture must work in seamless and powerful partnership with the headline and copy, forming an integrated whole where each element amplifies and reinforces the other for maximum persuasive impact.
chapters.takeaway: Use photos with story appeal that amplify the headline, keeping posters brutally simple and recognizable.
takeaways: Use photos with story appeal that amplify the headline, keeping posters brutally simple and recognizable.
The purpose of an image is to communicate the selling message, not merely to decorate the page.
Consistent art direction across a campaign builds critical brand recognition and memorability.

chapters.title: 9 How to Make Good Television Commercials
chapters.summary:
Ogilvy approached the powerful medium of television with the same unsentimental, direct-response, sales-driven discipline he applied to print media. The commercial's sole and non-negotiable purpose is to sell the product, not to win awards at festivals, impress peers, or merely entertain for entertainment's sake. He cataloged and rigorously ranked the most effective formats based on hard evidence and sales results. Topping his list was the product demonstration, citing the famous American Tourister luggage gorilla test as supreme proof that showing the product's claim being proven true in a dramatic, visual way is the most persuasive technique available. Other highly effective formats he validated included talking-head presentations from credible authorities, slice-of-life dramas depicting relatable situations, authentic testimonials, and clear problem-solution structures.

He issued critical, non-negotiable rules for every commercial: state the brand name early in the execution and repeat it consistently throughout, as viewer recall is fleeting and easily distracted. Show the packaging prominently and clearly to aid in-point-of-sale recognition. Open with a strong, compelling hook to capture attention within the first critical few seconds, as modern audiences are conditioned to flee from irrelevant content. Repeat key claims for reinforcement, understanding that message absorption requires repetition. He was scathingly critical of commercials that were so entertaining or clever that viewers remembered the joke, the music, or the celebrity but completely forgot which product was being advertised—ads that won creative kudos but failed miserably at the cash register.

Music, special effects, and all other gimmicks must serve comprehension and message retention, not distract from them. He advised testing television commercials with the same rigor and skepticism as print ads, measuring their ability to sell and drive action, not just their likability or memorability in focus groups. Finally, and perhaps most counter-intuitively, he stressed the importance of perseverance and discipline in media planning: a commercial that continues to sell and show a positive return on investment should not be retired simply because the agency team has grown tired of it or wants to try something new. Viewers develop commercial wear-out far later than the creators do, and replacing a proven, profitable performer with an untested new idea is an expensive and often reckless gamble.
chapters.takeaway: Make commercials that sell—demonstrate the product, name it often, and don't retire what works.
takeaways: Make commercials that sell—demonstrate the product, name it often, and don't retire what works.
The most effective commercial format is the product demonstration, which proves claims visually.
Entertaining commercials that fail to associate the entertainment with the product are a waste of money.

chapters.title: 10 How to Rise to the Top of the Tree
chapters.summary:
This chapter serves as Ogilvy's direct, practical, and often stern advice to young professionals ambitious to build a lasting and successful career in the advertising industry. His first and most fundamental counsel is to master the core disciplines and fundamentals before seeking accolades, titles, or public recognition. Learn to write with clarity, force, and persuasion. Learn the timeless principles of selling and human motivation. Understand the foundations and methodologies of market research. These are the essential tools of the trade, and without them, ambition is merely hollow posturing. Ambition itself should manifest not in political maneuvering for titles or status, but in the relentless, daily pursuit of exceptional, effective work. He believed "big shots are only little shots who keep shooting."

He recommends choosing your employer with great care—seek out an agency and a specific mentor with a proven reputation for training, for valuing craft, and for doing work you admire and want to emulate. Volunteer for the toughest, most challenging assignments, as they are the greatest opportunities to learn rapidly, stretch your capabilities, and prove your worth to the organization. Become indispensable to your team and your clients through sheer usefulness, reliability, and a consistent delivery of value. Specialize in what you genuinely love and are passionate about, but simultaneously maintain a holistic understanding of the entire business, from client relations and account strategy to media planning and production.

He emphasizes the absolute necessity of a powerful and sustained work ethic, recalling his own legendary long hours and expecting a similar level of devotion and passion in those who aspired to reach the top. He warned against the common and career-limiting pitfalls: job-hopping for marginal salary increases that signal a lack of commitment, developing a cynical or detached attitude toward the work and the clients, or coasting on past successes without continuing to learn and grow. True and lasting success in advertising, as exemplified in his own remarkable career, comes from the potent combination of disciplined craftsmanship and the courage to present bold, thoroughly researched ideas and to defend them tenaciously against timid thinking and bureaucratic inertia until your reputation for excellence becomes your most valuable and enduring professional asset.
chapters.takeaway: Rise by mastering fundamentals and doing fearless, excellent work—little shots become big shots by continuing to shoot.
takeaways: Rise by mastering fundamentals and doing fearless, excellent work—little shots become big shots by continuing to shoot.
Ambition should be channeled into producing excellent work, not into internal politics or title-seeking.
A strong work ethic and a willingness to tackle difficult assignments are essential for career advancement.

chapters.title: 11 Things I Hope to Find in Young People
chapters.summary:
Drawing from his decades of experience building one of the world's most respected agencies, Ogilvy enumerates the essential qualities and character traits he actively sought when hiring new talent, creating a detailed portrait of the ideal advertising professional. Paramount, above all else, were honesty and integrity, for the profession handles clients' significant fortunes, reputations, and livelihoods, and abuse of that trust is unforgivable. Intelligence was necessary, but it had to be combined with robust common sense—the practical wisdom to apply knowledge effectively in real-world situations. The capacity for sustained hard work over many years, not just bursts of effort, was a non-negotiable prerequisite.

He valued originality and a restless, imaginative mind, but always tempered by discipline and a respect for facts. A brilliant idea without the persistence, rigor, and follow-through to execute it properly is worthless. He looked for people with wide-ranging interests beyond the confines of advertising itself, believing a genuine curiosity about the world, about people, and about culture informed better and more resonant work. Good manners were important, as was the humility to accept criticism gracefully and to learn continuously from research, results, and feedback, rather than clinging stubbornly to one's own initial preconceptions or creative ego.

He prized enthusiasm that bordered on obsession, a deep and genuine love for the craft itself. He valued resilience in the face of the constant rejection that characterizes the client-driven advertising business, where most ideas die in meetings before they ever reach the public. And he sought the ability to collaborate effectively with colleagues and clients while simultaneously maintaining an independent, critical, and courageous perspective. He openly admitted to hiring misfits and eccentrics when they were demonstrably brilliant, preferring gifted irregulars to polished mediocrity. The ultimate portrait he painted was of a person who is fundamentally curious, industriously dedicated, scrupulously truthful, and who loves the daily work of advertising—its puzzles, its challenges, its victories—more than its superficial perks and status.
chapters.takeaway: Hire for integrity, curiosity, and obsessive love of the work—brilliant eccentrics beat polished mediocrity.
takeaways: Hire for integrity, curiosity, and obsessive love of the work—brilliant eccentrics beat polished mediocrity.
Discipline and persistence are as important as raw creativity in executing great ideas.
Resilience in the face of rejection is a necessary trait in the client-driven advertising business.

chapters.title: Can Advertising Sell Everything?
chapters.summary:
In his concluding and reflective chapter, Ogilvy confronts the ethical scope, moral boundaries, and social responsibility of his chosen profession. He expresses a firm, deeply held belief that advertising, when conducted with honesty, transparency, and based on truthful information, can be a powerful and constructive force for good in society. It can effectively sell almost any product or service that genuinely serves the buyer's interests and improves their life, from everyday household goods to political candidates and charitable causes. He pointed to successful campaigns for public health initiatives and environmental conservation efforts as compelling evidence of advertising's positive potential when harnessed for beneficial ends. Persuasion, in this enlightened view, is not inherently corrupting; it can and should inform and empower choice.

However, he draws clear and firm moral boundaries that should never be crossed. Advertising cannot sustainably sell products that consistently disappoint or betray the consumer, because the truth of the product experience inevitably surfaces through personal use and word of mouth, ultimately destroying any false promise built by clever campaigns. He expressed sincere pride in the positive outcomes that advertising has achieved over the decades—raising living standards by creating efficient mass markets for quality goods and services, and providing the financial engine that funds much of the free media ecosystem. Conversely, he voiced profound disdain for the abuses and failures of the craft, including deliberately deceptive claims and pandering to humanity's basest instincts for short-term gain.

He closes the book with his characteristic confidence, a confidence rooted in his life's work and empirical evidence. Research-guided, information-rich, and consumer-respectful advertising is both commercially potent and socially defensible. It works because it is built on a foundation of respect for the consumer's intelligence and their genuine needs. He urges his fellow practitioners to wield their considerable persuasive power seriously, ethically, and with a sense of duty. They must refuse work that would embarrass them or betray their principles if their role in creating it were publicly exposed, and they must recognize that the long-term health, credibility, and profitability of their profession depend entirely on maintaining the trust of the public they have the privilege to address.
chapters.takeaway: Advertising can sell nearly anything true and useful—but never sustainably sell what betrays the customer.
takeaways: Advertising can sell nearly anything true and useful—but never sustainably sell what betrays the customer.
Ethical advertising based on truth serves both commercial success and social responsibility.
Practitioners have a responsibility to refuse work that would compromise their integrity if exposed.
